# Evaluation

<!-- Generated by evaluation/make_evaluation_doc.py from evaluation/results/eval-v0110-20261029T201034Z.json. Do not edit by hand. -->

Numbers from `evaluation/results/eval-v0110-20261029T201034Z.json`: safeloadai 0.11.0, Python 3.13.17, Linux x86_64, 6203 files, run 20261029T201034Z. Every number on this page is generated from that file by `evaluation/make_evaluation_doc.py`; CI checks that the page is current.

## How to read the numbers

- **Positive** means the tool blocks the file for a reason about the file: SUSPICIOUS or MALICIOUS for safeloadai, "flagged" for the other scanners.
- **UNSUPPORTED** (the tool reads no format in the file) and **ERROR** (the tool itself failed; [ERRORS.md](ERRORS.md)) have their own columns. They are never a detection and never a miss, and they are left out of precision, recall and FPR. "skipped" is a file a scanner chose not to open.
- **TP** malicious and positive, **FN** malicious and CLEAN (a miss), **FP** benign and positive, **TN** benign and CLEAN. Files whose label is unclear are counted apart.
- precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN), FPR = FP / (FP + TN). The intervals are 95 % Wilson score intervals: with a few dozen files per cell they are wide, and they say so.
- safeloadai runs with its defaults (no options, the shipped known-file list on).

### Repository-name rule for proofs of concept

A Hub file is benign by selection: it comes from a popular-library stratum and the Hub's scanners do not flag it. That says nothing about a repository whose name declares a vulnerability proof of concept or a scanner test (words such as `poc`, `exploit`, `bypass`, `malicious`, `rce`, `payload`, `huntr` between separators in the repository id; `evaluation/batch_hf.py: DECLARED_POC`). Such a file is labelled unclear instead of benign. The rule looks at the repository name only, never at a verdict, but it was written after the first pass over hf-heldout2, when its results were known, so it is not blind. Every table that depends on labels is therefore also given without the rule (rows or columns marked "without PoC rule"), where these files count as benign.

| group | files the rule labels unclear |
|---|---|
| hf-unsafe | 3 |
| hf-heldout | 4 |
| hf-heldout2 | 8 |
| hf-heldout3 | 13 |
| **all** | **28** |

### An honest note on the malicious side

840 of the 903 malicious files (0.930) are our own lab payloads and their mutations. They are built to cover every technique we know of (public scanner bypasses rebuilt with marker payloads, every pickle encoding, every container), so they measure coverage of known techniques, not how often real attacks are caught. The real-world malicious files are the Hub files the Hub's scanners flag; there are few, many are proofs of concept rather than attacks, and their labels come from the Hub's evidence, not from ground truth. A recall of 1.0 on this corpus is therefore not a claim that safeloadai catches every attack: it says no file in this corpus got through.

### Tune and held-out split (overfitting)

The benign Hub corpus is split in two by a hash of the repository id (`evaluation/fetch_benign_hf.py: split_of`), so every file of one repository is on the same side and a repository's sibling files cannot leak into the other half. Allowlist reviews, policies, profiles and the known-file list were built from the tune half only (`evaluation/splits/hf-tune.txt`). The held-out half (`evaluation/splits/hf-heldout.txt`) is the false-positive rate we report. A large gap between the two FPRs is what overfitting to the tune half looks like. hf-heldout2 is a second held-out set from repositories no earlier corpus used, measured once with the final release.

### Bugs the held-out sets surfaced

The held-out rule (nothing is tuned on held-out files) is about the allowlists, policies and the known-file list. Bugs in the code that the held-out files showed were fixed: each was reproduced on a synthetic file of our own (a marker, never the Hub file), fixed in general and covered by a test. For files of these kinds the held-out measurement is no longer blind.

| kind | what was wrong | test |
|---|---|---|
| host memory | a large dill pickle made the static analysis on the host hold more than 13 GB (the listing for the dashboard); now bounded, and running out is ERROR E105 | `tests/test_resource_limits.py` |
| cloudpickle | a function or class pickled by cloudpickle was MALICIOUS without any sink (`builtins.type`, `staticmethod` and cloudpickle's helpers were treated as sinks); now the path of dill functions and Keras Lambdas | `tests/test_cloudpickle.py` |
| dill arrays | dill's `_create_array` (numpy array reconstruction) was a code-execution sink; now judged by its first argument | `tests/test_cloudpickle.py` |
| dill globals | dill's `__builtin__.__main__` (the globals of a pickled function) was a sink | `tests/test_cloudpickle.py` |
| emulation budget | large pickles ran out of the emulation's compute budget (ERROR E304); the budget now grows with the file, up to a fixed ceiling | `tests/test_emulation.py` |
| --validate-boosters (0.10.0) | a Booster stored in an `XGBClassifier`'s state was refused, because the walk for other uses of the class went into the stored instance and found its class; the option's column was scanned again after the fix (the default is not affected) | `tests/test_boosters.py` |

## What a user meets on held-out benign files

A false positive is not one thing. A *soft block* has only UNVERIFIABLE reasons and can be accepted item by item for that file; a *hard block* has a RISKY or MALICIOUS reason and cannot. The FPR here is soft plus hard blocks over the files in a format safeloadai reads (CLEAN, soft or hard).

- **default**: no options.
- **`--trust-inert-from`**: `--trust-inert-from scikit-learn --trust-inert-from transformers --trust-inert-from torch`, reading those libraries' source (the evaluation reads unpacked distributions, `run_eval.py --opt-in-site`). Every file is scanned again with it, so a verdict it makes stricter shows too.
- **`--validate-boosters`**: pickled XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost models whose model bytes pass the structural validator in the sandbox are accepted (off by default; docs/OPTIONS.md). Only files a Booster blocks are scanned again.
- **upper bound**: every UNVERIFIABLE item of every file accepted. Not a switch and not recommended: it is the most any override could clear.

## Why benign files are not CLEAN (root causes)

Every benign file that was not CLEAN in [`eval-v0110-20261029T201034Z.json`](../evaluation/results/eval-v0110-20261029T201034Z.json) (safeloadai 0.11.0), classified from the scan evidence alone by `evaluation/fp_anatomy.py`: the recorded reasons and the items outside the allowlist, never the file. A file with several causes counts once, under the first that applies in the order a, b, f, e, c, d (a file that also needs code its author wrote stays in the floor whatever else it needs). Whether a module belongs to a public library is checked against PyPI releases (archives read, never installed). Shares are of all benign files of the set.

| cause | hf-heldout2 | hf-heldout |
|---|---|---|
| **a** user-defined classes (`__main__`, modules in no public package) | 46 (1.6 %) | 10 (2.0 %) |
| **b** custom Keras objects registered by the model author | 73 (2.6 %) | 20 (4.0 %) |
| **c** classes from known public libraries missing from the allowlist | 168 (6.0 %) | 41 (8.3 %) |
| **d** old module paths of already reviewed classes | 1 (0.0 %) | 2 (0.4 %) |
| **e** data-only formats safeloadai does not parse (UNSUPPORTED) | 20 (0.7 %) | 2 (0.4 %) |
| **f** other (code in the file, emulation limits, structure, tool errors) | 40 (1.4 %) | 6 (1.2 %) |
| **irreducible floor (a + b)** | 119 (4.2 %) | 30 (6.0 %) |
| reducible by review (c + d) | 169 (6.0 %) | 43 (8.7 %) |
| benign files not CLEAN / benign files | 348 / 2806 | 81 / 496 |

**The irreducible floor.** Classes the model author wrote (a: `__main__` or a module in no public package) and custom Keras objects the author registered (b) exist only in the author's code. Rebuilding them runs that code, which safeloadai cannot read, so no allowlist can make such a file CLEAN without accepting arbitrary code. These files stay blocked by design, almost all as soft blocks that their owner can accept item by item (`--allow`, `safeloadai override`) after reading the code. On hf-heldout2 the floor is 119 of 2806 benign files (4.2 %).

**Reducible causes.** c (classes of public libraries the allowlist does not have yet) and d (older module paths of reviewed classes) are what allowlist review and the historical-path generator work on; e (formats safeloadai did not parse) is what the data-only validators address; f is everything else (code carried in the file, emulation limits, structural findings, tool errors). Of the c + d files on hf-heldout2, 85 need only classes whose state a native parser reads (XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost boosters); they stay off the allowlist (DECISIONS.md, Booster under A2).

f on hf-heldout2 by kind: structure 14, keras-lambda 10, serialized-code 10, call-gadget-or-code-module 7, emulation-anomaly 7, no-evidence-recorded 4, risky-reason-next-to-library-classes 1, tool-error 1.

## Limits of this evaluation

- The other scanners are measured on every file here, including formats they do not read; their errors, unsupported and skipped columns show that part. A detailed per-format comparison is withheld until coordinated disclosure with the affected projects is complete.
- Model backdoors and poisoned weights (OWASP LLM04) are not measured: a file scanner cannot see them ([THREAT_MODEL.md](THREAT_MODEL.md)).
- Regenerate this page after a new run: `python evaluation/make_evaluation_doc.py RESULT.json`.
